reply:
I fixed it in `loader.mjs`. `fetchAll` started every request inside `ids.forEach(async …)`, but `forEach` doesn't wait for async callbacks. So the function returned `results` straight away, often before any request had finished, and you got an empty list. The requests themselves still went out, which is why they showed up in the network log.

The fix is one line:
```js
return Promise.all(ids.map((id) => fetchOne(id)));
```
This waits for every request, and the results now come back in the same order as `ids`, as the doc comment promises. The old code added results in whatever order the requests finished.

I ran a quick test where the requests finished in reverse order. It returned `['u1','u2','u3']` in the right order.

I didn't add a permanent test or check the widget itself. One behaviour change: if a single request fails, `fetchAll` now fails with that error. Before, those failures were silently dropped.

reply:
I fixed the invoice maths in `invoice.mjs`. The tea towel invoice now prints tax 0.11 and total 1.51, and all 4 tests pass, including a new one for this case.

**Cause:** the code worked in floating-point dollars. In floating point, `1.40 * 7.5 / 100` comes out as `0.10499999…` rather than exactly 0.105. Rounding to two decimals then dropped it to 0.10 instead of rounding the half cent up. Prices whose tax lands exactly on a half cent can hit the same problem.

**Fix:** all the arithmetic now uses whole cents.
- Each price is converted to cents, then multiplied by the quantity.
- The tax rate is held as a whole number (7.5% becomes 750 hundredths of a percent). Tax is then rounded half-up to the cent using whole numbers only, as the README specifies, so it can't land just under a half cent.
- Amounts are only turned back into dollars for display.

**Test:** I added a test to `invoice.test.mjs` for the tea towel case (1.40 → tax 0.11, total 1.51).

**Limit:** a custom `taxPercent` is only honoured to two decimal places (e.g. 7.5 or 7.25). A rate like 7.125 would be rounded to 7.13. That doesn't affect the standard 7.5%.

Bang to rights: it was floating-point maths. In binary, `1.40 * 7.5 / 100` comes out as `0.10499999…`, so `toFixed(2)` rounded it down to 0.10 when it should have gone up to 0.11. The total had the same problem. That's why the 1.40 tea towel printed tax 0.10 and total 1.50.

The fix is in `invoice.mjs`. All the maths now works in whole cents:
- Each price is converted to cents with `Math.round(price * 100)` before it's multiplied by the quantity.
- The tax rate is held in hundredths of a percent (7.5% → 750). Tax is `floor((subtotalCents * 750 + 5000) / 10000)`, which is exact half-up rounding with integers only. That's the rule in the README.
- Amounts are only turned back into dollar strings at the end. `lineTotal` still returns dollars, so the printed invoice layout hasn't changed.

How I checked it:

Bob can now log in with "  Bob@Example.COM ". The new regression tests and the full suite pass (6 tests); I didn't run them against the old code to watch them fail first.

**Cause:** `normalize_email` in `accounts/util.py` is meant to produce the standard form of an address. Signup, login and invites all look accounts up by that form. But it only checked for an `@`. It didn't remove surrounding spaces or ignore capitals, so Bob's account was saved under `Bob@example.com` while login searched for `  Bob@Example.COM `. No account matched, so he got "invalid email or password".

**Fix:** that function now trims spaces and lowercases the address before splitting it at the `@`. Because signup, login and invites all use it, they now agree. It also stops someone signing up twice as `Bob@…` and `bob@…`.

**Tests added** in `tests/test_accounts.py`:
- Sign up as `Bob@example.com`, then log in with `"  Bob@Example.COM "`; this succeeds and returns `bob@example.com`.
- A second signup with ` bob@EXAMPLE.com` is rejected as a duplicate.

**Decision for you:** I lowercase the whole address, including the part before the `@`. Strictly, that part can be case-sensitive, but almost no real mail provider treats it that way. If you'd rather keep it, lowercasing only the domain and trimming spaces would still fix Bob's case.

It's quadratic. In `events.py:22-26`, `seen_list` is a **list**, so `e["id"] not in seen_list` walks through every ID seen so far, one comparison at a time.

- Each lookup costs O(u), where u is the number of unique IDs seen so far.

- With ~200k events that's about n²/2 ≈ 2×10¹⁰ string comparisons. Python does those in an interpreted loop, so it takes minutes, which fits the FIXME.
- An event whose ID was already seen early on can be found quickly. An event with a new ID always scans the whole list before it's appended, and new IDs are the common case.

`EMAIL_RE` (`validators.py:4`) is `^[^@]+@[^@]+$`, and `is_valid_email` runs it on `value.strip()` (`validators.py:9`). It only checks that the input contains exactly one `@`, with at least one character before it and at least one after. Neither side has any other restriction.

## What it accepts and rejects
I ran `is_valid_email` on these inputs:

| Input | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `bob@x.com` | accepted | one `@`, both sides non-empty |
| `bob@localhost` | accepted | no dot needed in the domain |
| `a@b` | accepted | same |
| `bob@@x.com` | rejected | two `@` |
| `a@b@c` | rejected | two `@` |
| `@x.com` / `bob@` | rejected | one side is empty |
| `a b@c d` | accepted | `[^@]` matches spaces |
| `a\nb@c` | accepted | `[^@]` matches newlines too |
| `' bob@x.com\n'` | accepted | `.strip()` removes the outer whitespace first |

## The three cases in the issue
None of them is a bug in the regex. The code does what it says, and the issue asks for policy changes.

- **`bob@localhost` and `a@b` accepted:** This is intended. Both are valid address syntax, because the email standards don't require a dot in the domain. Rejecting them would be a product choice: adding a "domain must contain a dot" rule would block those two inputs and nothing else. Syntax checks can't tell whether a domain is "real" anyway; only a confirmation email can. The tests (`test_validators.py`) only check `alice@example.com` passes and `alice.example.com` fails, so nothing states the intended strictness either way.
- **`bob@@x.com` rejected:** Correct. A validator shouldn't guess what the user meant and silently change it to `bob@x.com`. That could send mail to the wrong address. If anything is wanted here, it's a clearer error message or a "did you mean…?" hint in the form.

## Gaps the issue doesn't mention
- Spaces and other whitespace (including newlines) are accepted inside the address, e.g. `a b@c d` and `a\nb@c`. This is the real weakness. Matching `[^@\s]` on each side instead of `[^@]` would fix it.
- Nothing checks length or characters (no limit on the local part, no check that the domain is a valid hostname). That's acceptable for a loose check, but it should be a deliberate choice.

I didn't change any code. I'd answer #1423 with "works as designed" for its three examples, and open a separate issue for the whitespace problem if it matters.

Prices are "current", so a cache that never expires would keep serving old prices indefinitely. I'll use a time-limited cache with a size cap instead.

Adding tests for the edge cases that matter: repeat hits, TTL expiry, no caching of unknown SKUs, eviction. Tests also need cache isolation.

`get_price` in `prices.py` now caches prices, so it calls the pricing backend once per SKU instead of on every lookup. In a quick run of 300 lookups across 3 SKUs, the backend was called 3 times and the run took 0.15s; uncached, that would be about 15s. All 7 tests pass.

How it works:
- **Prices expire after 5 minutes** (`CACHE_TTL = 300`). The backend returns the "current" price, so a cache that never expires would keep serving old prices after a price change. A shorter TTL means fresher prices but more backend calls.
- **At most 10,000 SKUs are kept** (`CACHE_MAX_SIZE`). When it's full, the SKU used least recently is dropped.
- **Unknown SKUs aren't cached.** They still raise `KeyError` and are looked up again every time.
- **`prices.clear_price_cache()`** empties the cache when you need fresh prices immediately.
- **It's safe with threads.** A lock protects the cache, but the backend call happens outside it so one slow fetch doesn't hold up others. The catch is that two threads asking for the same uncached SKU at the same moment can both call the backend. That's harmless, just one extra call.

Tests (`test_prices.py`):
- Each test now starts with an empty cache and a reset call counter.
- New tests check four things: repeat lookups call the backend once, entries expire after the TTL, unknown SKUs aren't cached, and the least recently used SKU is the one dropped.

I also added a paragraph to `README.md` describing the cache.

Didn't do: 60s is my guess, so set it to however stale you can stand a price being. The cache has no size limit, which is fine for a normal-sized catalogue. Two threads asking for the same uncached SKU at once can both hit the backend; that's harmless, but it isn't locked against.

reply:
I fixed it in `loader.mjs`. `fetchAll` was returning before any of the API calls had finished. `ids.forEach(async …)` starts each fetch but doesn't wait for it, so `fetchAll` handed back `results` while it was still empty. That's why the calls showed up in the network log but the widget got no users. When results did arrive, they were added in whatever order the fetches happened to finish, not the order of `ids`.

The fix:
```js
return Promise.all(ids.map((id) => fetchOne(id)));
```
This waits for every fetch and keeps results in the same order as `ids`. One behaviour change: if any single fetch fails, `fetchAll` now fails too. Before, a failed fetch was silently lost.

I checked it with a quick Node run where the fetches took different times. `[3,1,2]` returned `['u3','u1','u2']`, which is the right length and the input order.

Problem: `paginate` uses `end = start + per_page - 1` with an exclusive slice, so each page drops its last item (#1010 on page 1, #1013 too on page 2).

Adding a regression test that checks every item shows up on exactly one page.

Fixed: order #1010 now appears as the last row of page 1.

**Cause:** the bug wasn't in `report.py`, which renders the screen. It was in the `paginate` helper in `listing.py`. That function worked out the end of each page as one less than it should have (`start + per_page - 1`) and then used Python's slice, which already leaves out the end position. So every full page lost its last order. Page 1 showed only #1001–#1009. Page 2 still ended at #1013 only because there were too few orders to fill it.

**Fix:** in `listing.py`, the page end is now `start + per_page`.

**Checks:**
- **Before the fix:** running `python3 report.py` showed page 1 ending at #1009 and page 2 starting at #1011.
- **After the fix:** page 1 shows #1001–#1010 and page 2 shows #1011–#1013.
- **Tests:** I added two tests to `test_listing.py`. One checks that 13 orders split into pages of 10 and 3, with every order shown once and in order. The other checks that a page past the end is empty. All 7 tests pass.

**Other screens:** any other report that uses `paginate` was dropping one row per full page in the same way. This fix covers those too.

Adding a regression test for Bob's case, including the duplicate-signup and invite paths that use the same key.

Bob can log in now: `"  Bob@Example.COM "` matches his `Bob@example.com` account. All 7 tests pass.

**Cause:** signup, login and invites all look accounts up by the address that `normalize_email` (in `accounts/util.py`) produces. That function only checked the address had an `@` in it. It didn't trim spaces or ignore capitals, so the address his password manager pasted never matched the one he signed up with.

**Fix:** `normalize_email` now trims spaces and lowercases the whole address. Because all three flows use it, they treat addresses the same way:
- **Login:** case and stray spaces no longer matter.
- **Signup:** someone can no longer make a second account by changing the capitals (`Bob@…` vs `bob@…`).
- **Invites:** the accepted address can differ in case or spacing from the one the invite was sent to.

**Tests:** I added three to `tests/test_accounts.py`, covering Bob's exact login, a duplicate signup that differs only in case, and an invite accepted with different case and spacing.

**Two things to know:**
- **Saved addresses:** accounts are now stored lowercased, so this returns `bob@example.com` instead of `Bob@example.com`. The store only lives in memory, so nothing already saved needs updating. If you later save accounts to a database, existing mixed-case entries will need lowercasing.
- **Lowercasing the part before `@`:** the email standard technically lets that part be case-sensitive. In practice almost no mail provider works that way, and lowercasing is the usual choice for login.

**Cause:** the `total` getter in `cart.mjs:14-16` calls itself.

```js
get total() {
  return this.total;   // reads the `total` getter again, so it recurses forever
}
```

Reading `this.total` inside the `total` getter runs the same getter again, with nothing to stop it. The stack overflows on the first read. In prod that read is `formatPence(cart.total)` in `app.mjs:8`, so every `/checkout` request crashes, whatever the order contains. The running sum is stored correctly in `this._total`, which the constructor sets and `add()` updates. The getter just reads the wrong name.

I reproduced it: a cart with one item at 250 × 2 throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` when `.total` is read, while `c._total` is `500`.

**Fix:** have the getter return the stored field:

```js
get total() {
  return this._total;
}
```

**Also worth doing:**
- The request handler in `app.mjs` has no try/catch around `checkout(order)`. An error thrown there ends up as an unhandled rejection in the async callback, and on Node 22 that kills the whole process. Catching it and returning a 500 would keep one bad code path from taking the server down.
- There are tests for `money.mjs` (`money.test.mjs`) but none for `Cart`. A single test that reads `cart.total` after an `add()` would have caught this.

```python
    seen_list = []
    ...

```

- Each membership check compares the id against every id already seen, so it costs O(k), where k is the number of unique ids so far.
- Over n events, the total cost is O(n·u), where u is the number of unique ids. Mostly-unique input makes that O(n²).
- With about 200k events, that is about 2×10¹⁰ string comparisons in the worst case (n²/2). Each one is an interpreted Python `==`, which explains the "several minutes" in the FIXME.

**Fix:** make `seen_list` a `set` and use `seen.add(...)`. Membership checks become O(1) on average, so the whole function is O(n). Output order stays the same, because `unique` is still a list built in input order. The existing test in `test_events.py:9` covers that ordering.

The three behaviours in #1423 are what the regex was written to do, so none of them is a regex bug. Two are a matter of policy, and one is a request we shouldn't take. I didn't change any code.

**What `EMAIL_RE` accepts** (`validators.py:4`, used at `:9` after `value.strip()`):

```
^[^@]+@[^@]+$
```

It accepts any string with exactly one `@`, at least one character before it and at least one after it, where neither side contains another `@`. It doesn't check anything else: no dots, TLD, character set or length limits.

I ran it against these inputs:

| Input | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `bob@x.com` | accepted | |
| `bob@localhost`, `a@b`, `.@.` | accepted | it doesn't require a dot or TLD in the domain |
| `a b@c d`, `a\nb@c` | accepted | `[^@]` also matches spaces and newlines inside the string |
| `bob@-x-.com` | accepted | it doesn't check the domain's syntax |
| `  bob@x.com  ` | accepted | `.strip()` removes the outer whitespace first |
| `bob@@x.com`, `a@b@c` | rejected | more than one `@` |
| `@x.com`, `bob@` | rejected | one side is empty |
| `"a@b"@x.com` | rejected | quoted local parts aren't supported, though RFC 5322 allows them |

Without `.strip()`, `$` would also match before a trailing `\n`. The strip already handles that case.

**The three reported items:**

1. **`bob@localhost` and `a@b` accepted.** The regex is designed to allow these, and RFC 5322 allows them too, since `localhost` and single-label domains are valid. Rejecting them is a product decision, for example requiring a dot in the domain. Even then, the format check would only reject them by shape; it can't tell whether a domain is real. Only DNS/MX lookups or a confirmation email can do that.
2. **`bob@@x.com` rejected.** This is correct. The reporter wants the validator to guess what the user meant and fix the typo. A validator shouldn't rewrite input: silently changing it can send mail to the wrong address. The right response is to reject it and show an error message.
3. **The vaguer "behave properly".** The real weaknesses are things the issue doesn't mention: it accepts spaces, newlines and control characters inside the address, and it doesn't check the domain's syntax. Of these, embedded whitespace and newlines are the strongest case for tightening, since a newline in an email address can enable header injection.

**Suggested resolution:** close items 1 and 2 as working as intended, or treat item 1 as a feature request if product wants a dot in the domain. If the validator is tightened, the useful change is to reject whitespace and control characters. Proof that an address actually exists should come from the confirmation email, not the regex.

I added a cache to `get_price` in `prices.py` that keeps each SKU's price for 60 seconds, so the backend is called at most once per SKU per minute. All 6 tests pass, including three new ones.

- **Why it expires:** the backend returns the *current* price, so a cache that never expires (like `lru_cache`) would keep serving old prices after they change. You can change the 60 seconds with `CACHE_TTL`, and `clear_price_cache()` empties the cache to force fresh lookups.

- Unknown SKUs are fetched again on every lookup.

I also added a short note to `README.md`.

Two limits to be aware of:
- The cache has no size limit, but it only grows with the number of distinct SKUs requested.
- It isn't locked against two lookups at the same moment. That's safe, but two simultaneous first lookups of one SKU can both call the backend.

- **Price changes show up late.** After a price changes in the backend, it can take up to 60 seconds to appear unless someone calls `clear_price_cache()`. If invoices need the exact live price, lower the time limit or clear the cache before invoicing.

- **Simultaneous lookups can duplicate a fetch.** If two threads miss the cache for the same SKU at the same moment, both call the backend. The result is still correct; it just costs one extra call.

**What changed in `client.py`:**
- A new `_timeout_from_env()` reads `CLIENT_TIMEOUT` as a number of seconds when the module is imported.
- If the variable is unset or blank, the timeout stays at 5s (`DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`).
- Bad values like `abc`, `0`, `-3`, `nan`, `inf` or `5s` raise a `ValueError` on import, so a typo in the deployment env fails at startup instead of silently using a wrong timeout.
- The README now documents the variable.

**Checks:** `python3 -m unittest` passes all 7 tests, including 4 new ones in `TimeoutConfigTest`. Running it directly: `CLIENT_TIMEOUT=30` gives `30.0`, unset gives `5.0`, and `5s` raises `ValueError: CLIENT_TIMEOUT must be a number of seconds, got '5s'`.

**Why I didn't build the full subsystem:**
- **YAML needs a new dependency.** The README says this is a "stdlib-only client" and `requirements.txt` says to keep the list short because it "ships inside the ops image." Python's standard library can't read YAML, so this would mean adding PyYAML to the ops image, and it isn't installed here.
- **Nothing would use the config file.** Ops are setting an env var, not shipping a file, so the loader and its search paths would be code nobody runs.
- **A singleton makes testing harder.** It's global state that tests would have to reset. The current pattern, where tests inject a fake `transport`, keeps them isolated.
- **It's easy to add later.** When a second setting actually needs a file, swapping `_timeout_from_env` for a config module touches one function. Building a framework around one setting means guessing what later settings will need.

- Letters that aren't accented forms of another letter get dropped, not transliterated. `"Ærøskøbing straße"` gives `rskbing-strae`.

I didn't check whether any existing posts actually have accented titles, and I didn't set up redirects.

```python
if e["id"] not in seen_list:
```

`seen_list` is a Python `list`, so `in` checks every element in order, which costs O(k) where k is the number of unique ids seen so far. Right, me old china. `EMAIL_RE = r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$"` (`validators.py:4`) is a loose check: exactly one `@`, with at least one non-`@` character on each side. That's all it checks. So all three things in the report are what the regex was written to do. None of them is a bug in the regex.

**What it accepts:**
- Anything at all except `@` on either side. That includes spaces, newlines, quotes and `<>`. `a b@c d`, `a\nb@c` and `<x>@""` all pass.
- A domain with no dot, like `localhost` or `b`.
- One trailing newline even without the strip, because Python's `$` matches just before a final `\n`. `EMAIL_RE.match("a@b\n")` is True. `is_valid_email` runs `.strip()` first anyway (`validators.py:9`), so spaces around the address are allowed too.

**What it rejects:** no `@`, more than one `@`, or nothing before or after the `@`. `@x.com`, `x@` and `bob@@x.com` all fail.

I ran each of these through `is_valid_email` and `EMAIL_RE.match`, and the results match the above.

**The three reported cases:**
1. `bob@localhost` accepted: works as written. It's also a valid address under RFC 5321, so rejecting it is a policy choice, not a fix.
2. `a@b` accepted: same reason, the domain has no dot. It's syntactically fine. If you want to require a dot in the domain, that's a new rule.
3. `bob@@x.com` rejected: this is correct. Silently treating it as `bob@x.com` would mean guessing what the user meant, and that's a bad idea. The form should reject it and show an error.

The existing tests (`test_validators.py`) only check `alice@example.com`, a missing `@`, and `nope`. Nothing in the code or tests says dotless domains should be rejected. So #1423 is a feature request for stricter rules, not a bug report.

There is a real weakness the issue doesn't mention. The regex allows spaces and newlines in the middle of an address, like `a b@c d`. If anything gets tightened, that's the part worth fixing. The usual check is still sending a confirmation email, not a smarter regex.

Ops can now set `CLIENT_TIMEOUT` in the deployment env to change the request timeout. I haven't built the full config subsystem (YAML loader, schema validation, `ConfigManager` singleton) yet, because I think it costs more than it's worth right now.

**Why I held off:**
- **New dependency in the ops image.** `README.md` says the client is "stdlib-only", and `requirements.txt` says "Keep this list short: the client ships inside the ops image." Python can't read YAML on its own, so we'd have to add PyYAML to that image.
- **Nothing would use it yet.** Ops only set an env var, and there's exactly one setting. A file loader, a schema and a singleton would all be code nobody calls. A global singleton would also make tests harder, since they'd have to reset shared state.
- **Easy to grow later.** `get_timeout()` is a single place to read config. When a second or third setting appears, it can become a small settings module, and if there's a real need for a config file then, it could be TOML (which Python reads without extra packages) or YAML.

**What changed:**
- `client.py`: `TIMEOUT` is now `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5.0`, and the new `get_timeout()` reads `CLIENT_TIMEOUT` on each request. If it's unset or blank, the default is used. Text that isn't a number, zero, negative values, `nan` and `inf` raise a `ValueError` that names the variable and the bad value.
- `test_client.py`: new tests check the default, that an override reaches the request, and that each kind of bad value is rejected.
- `README.md`: added a short Configuration section documenting `CLIENT_TIMEOUT`.

**Checks:** all 6 tests pass with `python3 -m unittest`. Running a request with `CLIENT_TIMEOUT=0.001` showed `get_timeout()` returning `0.001`. The request itself failed with a DNS error, as expected, because the internal billing host isn't reachable from here.

If you still want the full YAML-based subsystem and are OK adding PyYAML to the ops image, say so and I'll build it on top of this.

Invoice numbers now come out as `INV-00000042`. I did it with JavaScript's built-in `padStart` instead of adding `left-pad`, and all 4 tests pass.

**Why not `left-pad`:** the package is deprecated on npm, and `padStart` does the same thing (it's built into Node, and you're on Node 22). The README also says the project has no dependencies, and adding one would break that.

**What changed**
- In `invoice-number.mjs`, there's a new `DIGITS = 8` constant, and `formatInvoiceNumber` now returns `` `${PREFIX}${String(n).padStart(DIGITS, '0')}` ``.
- The email subject picks up the new format automatically, e.g. `INV-00000007 from Acme (GBP 123.45)`.
- Numbers longer than 8 digits are kept in full, not cut short (`INV-123456789`).
- `parseInvoiceNumber` needed no change. It reads both padded and old unpadded numbers (`INV-00000042` and `INV-42` both give 42), so invoices already issued still parse.
- I updated `test/invoice-number.test.mjs` to the padded format and added cases for 0, numbers over 8 digits, and the old unpadded format.

**Heads-up:** anything outside this repo that expects the `INV-42` style will now get `INV-00000042`. That includes stored strings, other systems and exact-match searches.

If you still want `left-pad` itself, it's a one-line swap plus `npm install left-pad`.

I fixed the accent bug using only Python's standard library. I didn't add the transliteration library or build the per-locale rules system, because neither is needed to fix this bug.

**What changed:** in `text.py`, `slugify` now splits each accented letter into its base letter plus the accent mark (Unicode NFKD normalisation), then drops anything that isn't plain ASCII. `"Crème Brûlée"` now becomes `creme-brulee`. All 4 tests pass, including a new `test_slugify_folds_accents`.

**Why I stopped there:**
- **The library:** accent-stripping already handles French, Spanish, German umlauts and most Latin text. A library adds a dependency to `requirements.txt` for cases you don't have yet.
- **Per-locale rules:** this would be built for languages nobody has asked for. It's easier to add when the first real need shows up, and you'll know then what the rules actually have to do.

**Known gap:** letters that aren't an accent on a base letter still get dropped. `"Straße Ølberg"` comes out as `strae-lberg`. If the blog will have titles like that, or non-Latin scripts, that's the point where Unidecode is worth adding. It would be a one-line change inside `slugify` and wouldn't need a locale framework. If you want it now anyway, I can add it.

**Risk to check:** `Post.url` is built from `slugify(title)`. Any post already published with an accented title will get a new URL, so links to the old one will break. If such posts exist, you'll need redirects from the old slugs or a stored slug for each post.
